{{nihongo|'''Kiyosi Itô'''|伊藤 清|Itō Kiyoshi|{{IPA|ja|itoː kiꜜjoɕi}}, 7 September 1915 – 10 November 2008}} was a Japanese [[mathematician]] who made fundamental contributions to [[probability theory]], in particular, the theory of [[stochastic process]]es. He invented the concept of [[stochastic integral]] and [[stochastic differential equation]], and is known as the founder of so-called [[Itô calculus]]. He also pioneered the connections between stochastic calculus and differential geometry, known as [[stochastic differential geometry]]. He was invited for the [[International Congress of Mathematicians]] in [[Stockholm]] in 1962.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://math.cornell.edu/international-congress | title=Cornellians at the International Congress of Mathematicians | publisher=[[Cornell University]] | access-date=16 June 2024}}</ref>
So much were  Itô's results useful to financial mathematics that he was sometimes called "the most famous Japanese in Wall Street".<ref name=jpntimes/>

Itô was a member of the faculty at [[University of Kyoto]] for most of his career and eventually became the director of their [[Research Institute for Mathematical Sciences]].  But he also spent multi-year stints at several foreign institutions, the longest of which took place at [[Cornell University]].

== Overview ==
[[File:Issei Shiraishi and Kiyoshi Ito 1935.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.9|Itô (right) with Issei Shiraishi in 1935. Shiraishi later became a mathematician.]]
Itô pioneered the theory of [[stochastic integration]] and [[stochastic differential equation]]s, now known as [[Itô calculus]]. Its basic concept is the [[Itô integral]], and among the most important results is a change of variable formula known as [[Itô's lemma]] (also known as the Itô formula). 
Itô also made contributions to the study of [[diffusion process]]es on [[manifold]]s, known as [[stochastic differential geometry]].

Itô calculus is a method used in the mathematical study of [[Stochastic process|random events]] and is applied in various fields, and is perhaps best known for its use in [[mathematical finance]]. In particular, the Itô's lemma's best known application is in the derivation of the [[Black–Scholes equation]] for option values.<ref name=jpntimes/>

Itô's methods are also used in other fields, including biology and physics.<ref name=jpntimes/> His results have been applied to [[population model]]s, [[white noise]], [[chemical reaction]]s, and [[quantum physics]], in addition to uses in various mathematical subjects such as [[differential geometry]], [[partial differential equation]]s, [[complex analysis]], and  [[harmonic analysis]] and [[potential theory]].<ref name="protter">{{cite journal | last=Protter | first=Philip | title=The Work of Kyoshi Itô | journal=Notices of the American Mathematical Society | volume= 54 | issue= 6 | pages=744–745 |date=June–July 2007 | url=https://www.ams.org/notices/200706/tx070600744p.pdf | format= }}</ref>

Fellow mathematician [[Daniel W. Stroock]] noted that "People all over realized that what Ito had done explained things that were unexplainable before."<ref name=lohr/> Economist [[Robert C. Merton]] stated that Itô's work had provided him "a very useful tool" in his own prize-winning work.<ref name=lohr/>

Although the standard [[Hepburn romanization]] of his name is ''Kiyoshi Itō'', he used the spelling Kiyosi Itô ([[Kunrei-shiki romanization]]). The alternative spellings Itoh and Ito are also sometimes seen in the [[Western world]].

Itô was married with three daughters.<ref name=lohr/>

==Biography==
[[File:Seizo Ito and Kiyoshi Ito cropped Seizo Ito Kiyoshi Ito Tsuyo Ito Seitaro Ito Seihachi Ito and Mishi Ito 1937.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.6|Kiyosi Itô (right) with his brother Seizō Itō in 1937. Seizō later became a mathematician.]]
Itô was born on 7 September 1915 in a farming area located west of [[Nagoya, Japan]],<ref name=lohr/> that being the town of [[Hokusei, Mie|Hokusei-cho]] in [[Mie Prefecture]].<ref name="times-obit">{{cite news | url=https://www.thetimes.com/article/professor-kiyosi-ito-mathematician-and-probability-theory-expert-bgwhnzm7p50 | title=Professor Kiyosi Itô: mathematician and probability theory expert | newspaper=[[The Times]] | location=London | date=20 November 2008 }}</ref> He excelled in his studies as a youth.<ref name=lohr/> Admitted to the [[Imperial University of Tokyo]], he studied mathematics and became interested in the underdeveloped field of [[probability theory]], graduating from there in 1938,<ref name="times-obit"/> with his degree in mathematics being granted by the [[Graduate School of Science and Faculty of Science, University of Tokyo|university's Faculty of Science]].<ref name="pastdirs-bio"/> 

[[File:Kiyoshi Ito 1940.jpg|thumb|right|Itô at the Cabinet Statistics Bureau in 1940]]
From 1939 to 1943 he worked as a Statistical Officer with the [[Statistics Bureau (Japan)|Statistics Bureau of the Cabinet Secretariat]],<ref name="pastdirs-bio"/> There he was given rein by management to continue his research.<ref name="times-obit"/> His breakthrough paper, "On Stochastic Processes", appeared in 1942.<ref name="cornell-luminaries"/> 
In 1943, he was appointed an assistant professor at [[Nagoya Imperial University]],<ref name="times-obit"/> where he benefited from discussions with the mathematicians [[Kōsaku Yosida]] and [[Shizuo Kakutani]].<ref name="ito-fw"/>
From investigations done during this period he published a series of articles in which he defined the [[stochastic integral]] and laid the foundations of the [[Itō calculus]]. 
Meanwhile, he received his [[Doctor of Science]] degree from the Imperial University of Tokyo in 1945.<ref name="pastdirs-bio"/>

These works were published despite the difficulties of life in [[Japan during World War II]], including problems accessing libraries and especially the loss of contact with Western mathematicians and the lack of awareness of results from them.<ref name="protter"/><ref name="times-obit"/>  For instance, the only other Japanese mathematician actively interested in  Itô's work during the war, [[Gisiro Maruyama]], read a mimeographed copy of a paper while in a military camp.<ref name="ito-fw"/> Scholarly activity during the [[Occupation of Japan]] had its difficulties; in one case, paper shortages were such that a lengthy Itô article could not be published in a Japanese journal and he had to arrange for an American journal to publish it instead.<ref name="ito-fw"/> Ito later referred to his time at Nagoya as having been during "the dark age of World War II and its aftermath."<ref name="ito-fw">{{cite book | editor-first=D. W. | editor-last=Stroock | editor2-first=S. R. S. | editor2-last=Varadhan | title=Kiyosi Itô Selected Papers | location=New York | publisher=Springer-Verlag | orig-date= 1987 | year=2014 | pages= xiii&ndash;xvii | chapter=Foreword | author-first=Kiyosi | author-last= Itô| isbn=978-1461496304 }}  Subsequently reproduced in {{cite book | url=https://books.google.com/books?id=cSUSUfvT3PoC&dq=%22as+i+heard+from+him+later%2C+he+read+it+in%22&pg=PA532 | title=Wolf Prize in Mathematics | volume=1 | editor-first=S S | editor-last=Chern | editor2-first=F | editor2-last=Hirzebruch | publisher=World Scientific | year=2000 | location=Singapore | pages=531&ndash;535 | isbn=978-981-02-3945-9 }}                  </ref>

[[Image:Kiyoshi Ito 1954.jpg|thumb|left|upright=0.6|Itô, 1954]]
After this period he continued to develop his ideas on stochastic analysis with many important papers on the topic.
In 1952, he became a professor at the [[University of Kyoto]].<ref name=jpntimes/> His most well-known text, ''Probability Theory'', appeared in 1953.<ref name="cornell-luminaries"/> 
Itô  remained affiliated with Kyoto until his retirement in 1979. <ref name="times-obit"/>  
However, beginning in the 1950s, Itô spent long periods of time away from Japan.<ref name=lohr/>  He was at the [[Institute for Advanced Study]] from 1954 to 1956 while on a [[Fulbright fellowship]];<ref name="pastdirs-bio"/> while there he worked closely with [[William Feller]] and [[Henry McKean]] who were at nearby [[Princeton University]].<ref name="ito-fw"/>  He was a professor at [[Stanford University]] from 1961 to 1964 and a professor at [[Aarhus University]] from 1966 to 1969.<ref name="pastdirs-bio"/> 

Then in 1969 Itô arrived at [[Cornell University]], where he was a professor of mathematics for six years until 1975.<ref name="cornell-luminaries">{{cite news | url= https://as.cornell.edu/news/celebrating-cornell-university-luminaries-mathematics-and-statistics | title=Celebrating Cornell University luminaries in mathematics and statistics | first=Louis | last=DiPietro | publisher=[[Cornell University College of Arts and Sciences]] | date=17 April 2024 }}</ref>  This was his longest stint outside Japan.<ref name="pastdirs-bio">{{cite web | url=https://www.kurims.kyoto-u.ac.jp/~kenkyubu/past-director/ito/ito-kiyosi.html | title=Past Directors: Kiyosi Itô(1915-2008) | publisher=[[Research Institute for Mathematical Sciences]], [[Kyoto University]] | access-date=8 January 2009 }}</ref>  Among the courses he taught at Cornell was one in Higher Calculus.<ref>{{cite book | url= | title=Cornell University Announcements: College of Arts and Sciences, 1974&ndash;75 | publisher=Cornell University | date=July 1, 1974 | page=127 }}</ref>

Itô wrote not only in  [[Japanese language|Japanese]] but also in [[Chinese language|Chinese]], [[German language|German]], [[French language|French]] and [[English language|English]].<ref name=lohr/> However, his ability to converse in foreign languages was a different matter, and by his own admission his accent made him largely incomprehensible to Americans.<ref name=lohr>{{citation |last=Lohr |first=Steve |title=Kiyosi Ito, 93, Mathematician Who Described Random Motion, Dies  | newspaper=[[The New York Times]] |date=23 November 2008 |url=https://www.nytimes.com/2008/11/24/business/24ito.html?_r=1}}</ref>

When Itô left Cornell and returned to the University of Kyoto, he served as director of their [[Research Institute for Mathematical Sciences]].<ref name=jpntimes/> After his retirement, he became professor emeritus at Kyoto University.<ref name=jpntimes/> He also had a post-retirement position as a professor at the private [[Gakushuin University]] for several years,<ref name="pastdirs-bio"/> a common practice among higher-ranking Japanese academics.<ref name="times-obit"/> 

[[Image:Kiyoshi Ito 19911212 large.jpg|thumb|right|upright=0.7|Itô c. 1991]]

Itô  was recipient of the [[Wolf Prize in Mathematics|Wolf Prize]]  and the [[Kyoto Prize]].<ref name=lohr/>
He was a member of the [[Japan Academy]],<ref name="pastdirs-bio"/> and also a foreign member of the [[Académie des sciences]] in France and the [[National Academy of Sciences]] in the United States. <ref name=lohr/>

In his later years, Itô struggled with poor health.<ref name="times-obit"/>
Itô was awarded the inaugural [[Gauss Prize]] in 2006 by the [[International Mathematical Union]] for his lifetime achievements.<ref name=jpntimes/> As he due to his health was unable to travel to [[Madrid]], his youngest daughter, [[Junko Ito]], received the Gauss Prize from [[King Juan Carlos I]] on his behalf.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.alamy.com/junko-ito-left-daugther-of-japanese-mathematician-kiyoshi-ito-receives-the-gauss-prize-from-spanish-king-juan-carlos-i-during-the-opening-ceremony-of-the-international-congress-of-mathematicians-celebrated-in-madrid-tuesday-aug-22-2006-ap-photobernat-armangue-image541346179.html | title=Junko Ito, left, daughter of Japanese mathematician Kiyoshi Ito, receives the Gauss Prize from Spanish King Juan Carlos I during the opening ceremony of the International Congress of Mathematicians celebrated in Madrid Tuesday, Aug. 22, 2006. (AP Photo/Bernat Armangue) | publisher= [[Alamy]] | access-date=16 June 2024 }}  See also {{cite web | url=https://av.tib.eu/media/15952 | title=Gauss prize lecture - On Kiyosi Itô's work and its impact | publisher=[[TIB AV-Portal]] | access-date=16 June 2024 }}</ref> Later, IMU President [[Sir John Macleod Ball]] personally presented the medal to Itô at a special ceremony held in Kyoto.<ref>{{cite web | url=https://www.kyoto-u.ac.jp/en/about/honors/international-awards/gauss-prize | title=Dr. Kiyoshi Ito receives Gauss Prize | publisher=[[Kyoto University]] | access-date=16 June 2024}}</ref>
In October 2008, Itô was honored with Japan's [[Order of Culture]], and an awards ceremony for the Order of Culture was held at the Imperial Palace.<ref>{{cite news | url=http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/national/20081029TDY01304.htm |title=Donald Keene, 7 others win Order of Culture | archive-url=https://web.archive.org/web/20081030050218/http://www.yomiuri.co.jp/dy/national/20081029TDY01304.htm |archive-date=30 October 2008 | newspaper=[[Yomiuri Shimbun]]| date= 29 October 2008 | language=English }}</ref>  

Itô died on November 10, 2008, in [[Kyoto, Japan]], at age 93, of [[respiratory failure]].<ref name=jpntimes>{{cite news |title=Renowned math wiz Ito, 93, dies | newspaper=[[The Japan Times]] |date=15 November 2008 |url=https://www.japantimes.co.jp/news/2008/11/15/national/renowned-math-wiz-ito-93-dies/ | agency=[[Kyodo News]]}}</ref>
